To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
DNA methylation at growth related genes correlates with birth weight, and that these genes may be linked to developmental origins adult disease.
DNA methylation levels at 23 genes explain 70-85% of the variance of birth weight in a human cohort of newborns.
we have identified 23 genes with DNA methylation differences that explain 70-85% of the variance for birth weight in newborns.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel genes and pathways involved in growth and development and their potential association with birth weight and long term health outcomes.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the relationship between birth weight and adult health and disease.
the identification and characterization of genes involved in the regulation of human growth.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the DNA methylation differences at these growth related genes correlate well with birth weight and that these differences are more predictive of birth weight than gene expression levels at a single time point.

DNA methylation levels of growth related genes in cord blood are correlated with birth weight and that these methylation differences may reflect differences in transcriptional potential throughout development and that this may explain more of the variance in human birth weight than does single time point measurements of expression.

DNA methylation is a marker of gene expression potential at growth related genes and that this marker may be more useful than single time point measurements of expression for the study of complex traits.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the epigenetic state of a gene may be more important than the expression state in determining birth weight.

we have identified a novel molecular signature for birth weight, a complex quantitative trait, that can be used to identify novel genes and pathways in the developmental origins of adult health and disease.

we have identified a set of genes that can explain a large portion of the variance in human birth weight and that this is the first time that DNA methylation has been shown to be such an effective predictor of birth weight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
DNA methylation is a more robust biomarker of gene expression potential than gene expression itself.
we have identified a set of genes that may be important for birth weight determination and that these genes may be useful for future studies of the developmental origins of adult diseases.
DNA methylation is a much more sensitive measure of birth weight related gene expression than single time point transcript measurements.
